kcet|Chemistry|2006|42||0|0.s:
Optical activity needs a **chiral carbon** — one carrying four *different* groups.
Examine each compound for such a carbon.
(1) (CH₃)₂CH–CHO — the central CH carries two identical methyls, so not chiral.
(2) CH₃CH₂CH₂CHO — every carbon carries at least two hydrogens; no chiral centre.
(4) CH₃CH₂CBr₂CHO — that carbon carries **two** bromines, so two of its four groups are the
same; not chiral.
(3) CH₃CH₂CHBr–CHO — look at the carbon bearing the bromine. Its four attachments are:
  –H, –Br, –C₂H₅ and –CHO
All four are different, so it is a stereocentre and the molecule exists as a pair of
non-superimposable mirror images.
∴ CH₃CH₂CHBr–CHO.

kcet|Chemistry|2006|46||0|0:
Sodium hydrogencarbonate is a weak base, and it only liberates CO₂ from an acid **stronger**
than carbonic acid:
RCOOH + NaHCO₃ ⇒ RCOONa + H₂O + CO₂↑
Carboxylic acids have pKa around 4–5, comfortably stronger, so they all fizz:
(1) salicylic acid ✓, (3) benzoic acid ✓, (4) 4-nitrobenzoic acid ✓ — the nitro group makes
this one stronger still.
(2) **Phenol** has pKa ≈ 10, far weaker than carbonic acid (pKa ≈ 6.4). It is acidic enough to
dissolve in NaOH but not in NaHCO₃, so no CO₂ is evolved.
That difference is exactly why the bicarbonate test distinguishes a carboxylic acid from a
phenol in the laboratory.
∴ phenol.

kcet|Chemistry|2006|47||0|0.s:
This is the **Reimer–Tiemann reaction**.
Alkali first generates the electrophile from chloroform:
CHCl₃ + OH⁻ ⇒ CCl₃⁻ + H₂O, then CCl₃⁻ ⇒ :CCl₂ + Cl⁻
:CCl₂ is dichlorocarbene — a carbon with only six valence electrons, so strongly electron
deficient.
The phenoxide ion, which is electron rich, attacks it at the **ortho** position. Hydrolysis of
the resulting benzal chloride, –CHCl₂, then gives the aldehyde group:
C₆H₅OH + CHCl₃ + 3NaOH ⇒ 2-HO–C₆H₄–CHO + 3NaCl + 2H₂O
The product is salicylaldehyde, 2-hydroxybenzaldehyde.
Salicylic **acid** (1) would come from Kolbe's reaction, using CO₂ under pressure instead of
chloroform — a useful pair to keep straight: CHCl₃ gives the aldehyde, CO₂ gives the acid.
∴ salicylaldehyde.

kcet|Chemistry|2006|48||0|0:
Dry distillation of a calcium carboxylate gives a carbonyl compound, and the two groups
flanking the C=O come from the two carboxylate ions.
With a mixture of calcium benzoate and calcium acetate, the **mixed** product is the one
asked for:
benzoate contributes C₆H₅–
acetate contributes CH₃–
So the mixed ketone is C₆H₅–CO–CH₃, acetophenone ✓
The symmetrical products also form:
benzoate + benzoate ⇒ C₆H₅COC₆H₅, benzophenone (3)
acetate + acetate ⇒ CH₃COCH₃, propanone
Neither (2) benzaldehyde nor (4) acetaldehyde can form, because an aldehyde requires a
hydrogen next to the carbonyl, which only calcium **formate** could supply.
∴ acetophenone.
kcet|Chemistry|2006|49||0|0:
Hydrolysis gives benzoic acid only if the group attached to the ring already contains the
carbon that becomes –COOH.
(1) Phenyl cyanide, C₆H₅CN — the nitrile carbon hydrolyses straight to the carboxyl:
C₆H₅CN + 2H₂O ⇒ C₆H₅COOH + NH₃ ✓
(2) Benzoyl chloride, C₆H₅COCl — the acid chloride hydrolyses at once:
C₆H₅COCl + H₂O ⇒ C₆H₅COOH + HCl ✓
(4) Methyl benzoate, C₆H₅COOCH₃ — ester hydrolysis gives the acid and methanol ✓
(3) Benzyl chloride, C₆H₅CH₂Cl — the chlorine is on an sp³ carbon bearing two hydrogens, not
on a carbonyl. Hydrolysis is a simple nucleophilic substitution and gives **benzyl alcohol**,
C₆H₅CH₂OH. Reaching benzoic acid from there needs a separate oxidation.
∴ benzyl chloride.

kcet|Chemistry|2006|52||0|0.s:
Fats and oils are **triglycerides** — triesters of glycerol with three long-chain fatty acids.
Each of glycerol's three hydroxyls condenses with the –COOH of a fatty acid, losing water
and leaving the ester linkage –CO–O–:
CH₂–O–CO–R
|
CH–O–CO–R′
|
CH₂–O–CO–R″
So the characteristic group is the **ester** group ✓
The others belong elsewhere: a peptide group (1) is the –CO–NH– of proteins, an alcoholic
group (3) belongs to glycerol before it is esterified, and a ketonic group (4) does not appear
at all.
This is also why fats are hydrolysed by alkali — saponification simply breaks those ester links
to give soap and glycerol.
∴ an ester group.

kcet|Chemistry|2006|53||0|0.s:
Glycine is an amino acid, so it carries both an acidic –COOH and a basic –NH₂. Which form
dominates depends on the pH compared with the isoelectric point.
For glycine the isoelectric point is pI = 5.97. At that pH it exists as the neutral **zwitterion**,
H₃N⁺–CH₂–COO⁻, with no net charge.
The solution here is at **pH 4**, which is *below* the isoelectric point — so the medium is more
acidic than glycine's neutral point.
In excess acid the carboxylate is protonated:
H₃N⁺–CH₂–COO⁻ + H⁺ ⇒ H₃N⁺–CH₂–COOH
The molecule now carries a net **positive** charge and would migrate to the cathode in
electrophoresis.
Option (1), the zwitterion, is the form at pH 5.97, not at pH 4.
∴ H₃N⁺–CH₂–COOH.

kcet|Chemistry|2006|56||0|0:
In the brown ring test the nitrate solution is mixed with freshly prepared FeSO₄, and
concentrated H₂SO₄ is poured gently down the side so that it forms a layer underneath.
At the junction of the two layers the sulphuric acid liberates nitric acid, and the Fe²⁺
**reduces the nitrate to nitric oxide**:
6FeSO₄ + 3H₂SO₄ + 2HNO₃ ⇒ 3Fe₂(SO₄)₃ + 4H₂O + 2NO
Nitrogen goes from +5 in NO₃⁻ down to +2 in NO — that reduction is the essential step.
The NO so formed is then taken up by unreacted Fe²⁺ as a complex:
FeSO₄ + NO ⇒ [Fe(H₂O)₅NO]SO₄
and it is this nitrosyl complex, brown in colour, that forms the ring at the interface.
So it is the reduction of nitrate to NO, not any oxidation (2) or the action of the acid (4),
that the test depends on.
∴ the reduction of nitrate to nitric oxide.

kcet|Chemistry|2006|57||0|0.s:
The acrolein test detects **glycerol**, either free or combined.
The substance is heated with potassium hydrogen sulphate, KHSO₄, which acts as a
dehydrating agent. Glycerol loses two molecules of water to give acrolein, an unsaturated
aldehyde with a sharp, pungent, irritating smell:
CH₂OH–CHOH–CH₂OH ⇒ CH₂=CH–CHO + 2H₂O
Fats and oils are triesters of glycerol, so heating them with KHSO₄ frees the glycerol and
produces that characteristic smell ✓
The other options contain no glycerol: polysaccharides and reducing sugars are carbohydrates,
and proteins are polymers of amino acids. None of them gives acrolein.
∴ oils and fats.

kcet|Chemistry|2005|1||0|0.s:
Enthalpy and internal energy are related by
ΔH = ΔE + Δn(g)RT
where Δn(g) is the change in the number of **moles of gas**.
The reaction is 2CO(g) + O₂(g) ⇒ 2CO₂(g):
moles of gas on the left = 2 + 1 = 3
moles of gas on the right = 2
Δn(g) = 2 − 3 = **−1**
Substituting:
ΔH = ΔE + (−1)RT = ΔE − RT
Since RT is a positive quantity, ΔH is **smaller** than ΔE.
Physically: the gas volume shrinks, so the surroundings do work *on* the system, and that
work is why the heat released at constant pressure is less than the energy change at constant
volume.
The capacity of the vessel (4) is irrelevant — only the change in moles of gas matters.
∴ ΔH < ΔE.

kcet|Chemistry|2005|2||0|0.s:
A refrigerator works on the Joule–Thomson effect. The liquefied refrigerant is forced through
a narrow throttle valve into the low-pressure coils inside the cabinet, where it **expands**
and evaporates.
As the gas expands, its molecules move further apart against their own attractive forces.
Doing that work costs energy, which is taken from the kinetic energy of the molecules
themselves — so the gas cools sharply.
The cold gas then absorbs heat from the food, and the compressor outside recompresses it,
releasing that heat to the room through the condenser coils at the back.
So the cooling comes from the expansion, not from any chemical reaction of the refrigerant
(1) — the gas is chosen precisely because it is chemically inert and simply cycles round
unchanged.
∴ the expansion of the gas in the refrigerator.

kcet|Chemistry|2005|6||0|0:
Set out an ICE table for H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI.
Initial: H₂ = 15, I₂ = 5.2, HI = 0
At equilibrium HI = 10 mol. Since 2 HI form from 1 H₂ and 1 I₂:
H₂ consumed = 10/2 = 5 mol
I₂ consumed = 10/2 = 5 mol
Equilibrium amounts:
H₂ = 15 − 5 = 10
I₂ = 5.2 − 5 = 0.2
HI = 10
Now write Kc. The number of moles of gas is the same on both sides, so volume cancels and
moles may be used directly:
Kc = [HI]²/([H₂][I₂]) = 10²/(10 × 0.2) = 100/2 = 50
Notice how nearly all the iodine is used up — it is the limiting reagent, which is why its
equilibrium amount is so small and the constant so large.
∴ 50.
kcet|Chemistry|2005|7||0|0:
Start with 1 mole of N₂O₄ and let x be the fraction that dissociates.
N₂O₄ ⇌ 2NO₂
Initially: 1 mole of N₂O₄, no NO₂.
At equilibrium:
N₂O₄ remaining = 1 − x
NO₂ formed = 2x, since each N₂O₄ gives **two** NO₂
Total number of molecules = (1 − x) + 2x = **1 + x**
The check is at the limits: if nothing dissociates, x = 0 and the total is 1 ✓; if everything
dissociates, x = 1 and the total is 2, which is right because one N₂O₄ has become two NO₂ ✓
This increase in the number of particles is why the dissociation of N₂O₄ can be followed by
measuring the pressure, or the apparent molar mass, of the mixture.
∴ 1 + x.
kcet|Chemistry|2005|11||0|0:
The two constants are linked by
Kp = Kc(RT)^Δn
where Δn is the change in the number of moles of **gas**.
For N₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2NO(g):
moles of gas on the left = 1 + 1 = 2
moles of gas on the right = 2
Δn = 2 − 2 = **0**
Anything raised to the power zero is 1, so
Kp = Kc × (RT)⁰ = Kc × 1 = Kc = 0.1
So when the number of gas molecules does not change, Kp and Kc are numerically equal, and
neither the temperature nor the value of R is needed.
That is why the equilibrium concentrations given (0.5 mol each) are not required either —
they are there as a distraction.
∴ 0.1.

kcet|Chemistry|2005|12||0|0.s:
All three factors listed genuinely control how much gas a solid adsorbs.
**Nature of the gas** — a gas that is easily liquefied, with a higher critical temperature, has
stronger intermolecular attractions and is adsorbed more readily. SO₂ is adsorbed far more
than H₂ on the same charcoal.
**Pressure** — adsorption reduces the number of free gas molecules, so by Le Chatelier
raising the pressure drives it forward. This is the Freundlich isotherm, x/m = kP^(1/n).
**Temperature** — adsorption is exothermic, so cooling favours it and heating causes
desorption.
To these one could add the nature and surface area of the adsorbent, which is why charcoal
is activated.
Since each option is correct on its own, the answer must be the one that includes them all.
∴ all are correct.
